A more accurate term for this way of reading the Bible would be, not literally, but univocally. Univocal refers to a one to one correspondence. No room for analogy or poetic description. This would lead to some difficulties in certain passages.

For example, in Isaiah 59, it speaks of God strapping on his armor: a helmet, breastplate, sword, shield, etc. So let me ask you: does God actually put on armor? Does he have a body? So does God NEED armor? No. Obviously not. So is the Bible LYING when it says that God straps on armor? Obviously not. So what does it mean then? It means God is preparing for war, which means God is about to unleash his wrath, take vengeance, etc. It’s a warning. But it’s a warning given through an analogy.

So why doesn’t it just say it in simple terms? Because it’s literature. Actually it’s some of the most sophisticated and elegant literature there is. Here, in Isa 59, as in many places, it speaks of God as if he were a man because MEN are who he’s talking to. He wants us to get the point. The Bible therefore speaks to us in what’s called accommodating language. It’s like a parent speaking to a child. You enter into their world and speak to them on their level so that they understand.
